newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Cricket-Chandler blasts Wellington's 200th ton.
newsitem.headline: Cricket-Chandler blasts Wellington's 200th ton.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Nov 26 - Phil Chandler entered Wellington cricket's history books when scoring the province's 200th first-class century to set up a significant score against Auckland in the Shell Trophy opener at the Basin Reserve yesterday.
Having posted his maiden first-class century, Chandler continued on to be 111 not out at stumps with Wellington on 213 for three, 94 runs ahead of Auckland.
Chandler admitted he needed to look hard at his batting after struggling in the Trophy section of the Shell series last summer.

"I had some early mornings during the winter here at the indoor wicket at the Basin with Johnny A (Aiken). He came up with different ideas and we tried them out until I felt comfortable with them," Chandler said.
"I had a fairly good Shell Cup season last year but found it difficult to make the transition back to four-day play," he said.
Chandler was also predominantly a leg-side player, which opposing sides worked out quickly to restrict his scoring chances.
But the evidence of change was clear yesterday. Several times he charged the bowling as witnessed by the 17 boundaries in his 100.
The innings took 195 minutes and 162 balls and was just the anchor role needed by Wellington to allow them to shut Auckland out of the game today.
Roger Twose, who scored a quick 63 off 77 balls, also passed 8000 runs when reaching 42.

Auckland, a vastly different combination from that which beat Wellington in last year's Shell Trophy final with only five of those players in the Capital, struggled to score their 119 runs and were all out 27 minutes after lunch.
The Wellington attack had the benefit of a pitch with some juice to encourage the fast-medium home attack of Stephen Hotter, Richard Petrie and Heath Davis.
But apart from an opening stand of 49 runs, dominated by Richard Jones, the Auckland effort was lamentable.
Hotter, especially, relished the conditions and his four for 33 from 17 overs resulted from an unrelenting assault on the batsmen with both pace and bounce providing constant worries.
